nameStory: The "tick-trefoil" name comes from this plant's sneaky hitchhiking habit – its flat, sticky seed pods cling to your clothes and pet fur just like ticks! The "pointed-leaved" part refers to the sharp tips on its three-part leaves (trefoil means "three leaves"), while some folks call it "beggar's lice" because those clingy seeds seem to beg for a ride wherever you're going.
description: Pointed-leaved tick-trefoil is a woodland wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall with a somewhat sprawling habit. It has the classic three-part leaves typical of the legume family, each leaflet ending in a sharp point. In mid to late summer, it produces delicate pink to purple pea-like flowers in loose clusters at the top of the plant. After flowering, it develops the infamous flat, jointed seed pods that will stick to anything that brushes against them.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves (leaflets) with each leaflet ending in a distinct sharp point, giving them an almost heart-shaped appearance with a drawn-out tip

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple pea-like flowers arranged in loose, branching clusters at the stem tips, blooming from mid-summer into early fall

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, jointed seed pods that break apart into sticky segments – run your finger along them and feel how they want to cling to everything

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Somewhat floppy or leaning stems that may sprawl or lean against other plants, reaching 2-4 feet in height

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems feel slightly sticky or tacky to the touch, especially near the top where flowers and seed pods develop

habitat: Look for pointed-leaved tick-trefoil in rich, moist woodlands and forest edges throughout New England, particularly in deciduous and mixed forests. It prefers partially shaded areas with well-drained soil and is often found along woodland trails, in clearings, and at the borders between forest and field.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with the characteristic three-part leaves, but plants remain relatively small and inconspicuous in early season.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid to late summer with pink-purple flowers appearing in loose clusters. Plants reach full height during this time.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the notorious sticky seed pods develop and mature, ready to hitchhike on passing animals and hikers. Leaves may turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only dried stems with empty seed pod fragments clinging to the dead stalks.

funFact: This plant is basically nature's velcro – the inspiration for modern hook-and-loop fasteners actually came from studying how burdock seeds stick to fur, and tick-trefoil pods use a similar strategy with tiny hooks that grab onto fabric and animal fur with surprising tenacity!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with naked-flowered tick-trefoil, but that species has flowers that emerge directly from the base of the plant rather than from the leafy stems. Memory trick: pointed-leaved tick-trefoil is "properly dressed" with flowers coming from leafy stems, while naked-flowered is "undressed" with bare flower stalks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name "beggar's lice," this plant has no relation to actual lice – early settlers just used this term for any small, annoying thing that stuck to their clothes. The scientific name "glutinosum" literally means "sticky" or "glue-like," referring to those persistent seed pods.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative naked-flowered tick-trefoil, pointed-leaved tick-trefoil has flowers that emerge from the leafy stems rather than on separate stalks from the base. The leaf shape is also more distinctly pointed, and the overall plant tends to be taller and more robust. Both species have the same sticky seed pod strategy, but pointed-leaved tick-trefoil's flowers are more integrated with the leafy plant structure.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pointed-leaved tick-trefoil, its closest relative in New England, has flowers and leaves on the same stem - never the naked flower stalks that make this species so distinctive.
